Q1.answer: The paper studies whether normalizing each input window of a forecaster with its own recent statistics (per-window re-estimation of the mean/sd used for z-scoring, called RWN) reduces forecasting error when the level of the series shifts after training, while not harming accuracy when no shift occurs. It also asks how much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt the statistics versus a single re-estimation.
Q1.missing: Stated only through heavy acronyms (RWN, LS, TSD-anchored z-scoring) that are never expanded.

Q2.answer: Deployed forecasting systems encounter level shifts, and standard pipelines z-score inputs with statistics anchored to the training data; once the level shifts post-deployment, the fixed moments mis-scale the inputs and inflate error. So a normalization scheme robust to level shift would improve deployed accuracy.
Q2.missing: Both motivating premises (prevalence of level shifts; that TSD-anchored z-scoring is standard practice) are flagged [CITATION NEEDED], so the importance is asserted, not evidenced.

Q3.answer: In evaluations the authors examined, moment staleness (stale normalization statistics) and capacity insufficiency (model too small) are confounded, so prior gains cannot be attributed to fixing staleness. The paper deconfounds them by matching model capacity across conditions.
Q3.missing: The gap rests on a literature claim explicitly marked [CITATION NEEDED: literature search not yet run], so the confound is asserted without cited support.

Q4.answer: On a synthetic hourly load generator (SynthLoad) they injected piecewise level shifts of magnitude s ∈ {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}σ after the training period and compared three normalization schemes with a capacity-matched MLP: Baseline (training-set moments), RWN (trailing-48-window moments), and RWN-F (moments frozen after the first post-shift window). They measured MAE (mean ± sd over 5 seeds) on the test period in both no-shift (IID) and shifted (LS) conditions.
Q4.missing: 'PCM' and 'TSD' are never expanded; the exact level-shift injection mechanism is not fully specified.

Q5.answer: Capacity matching (iso-budget MLP) was chosen to separate the effect of stale normalization statistics from model capacity. Synthetic data with controlled shift injection was used to isolate the level-shift effect. The RWN-F ablation (freezing statistics after the first post-shift window) was designed to separate the value of one-shot re-estimation from continued adaptivity.
Q5.missing: No justification for the specific window length (48) or MLP hyperparameters; window is later admitted to be untuned.

Q6.answer: Experiments on SynthLoad (hourly generator with daily and weekly components plus additive Gaussian noise). Conditions: an IID (no-shift) run and level-shift runs at s = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8σ. Three schemes compared (Baseline, RWN, RWN-F). Backbone MLP with h=64, input L=168, horizon H=24, iso-budget, 5 random seeds; MAE reported as mean ± sd on the test period.
Q6.missing: RWN-F is only reported at s=0.6σ, not across all shift magnitudes.

Q7.answer: IID parity: RWN 0.409±0.007 vs Baseline 0.412±0.006. Under level shift RWN stays near IID level while the baseline degrades monotonically; at s=0.6σ MAE improves 0.641→0.452, and across 0.2–0.6σ the reduction is 11–29% with sd ≤ 0.012 (seed-stable ordering). At s=0.8σ, 0.712±0.021 (RWN) vs 0.731±0.015 (Baseline), a ~1 sd difference, so no gain claimed. RWN-F at 0.6σ = 0.518, so ~two thirds of the gain is from one-shot re-estimation and ~one third from adaptivity.
Q7.missing: Per-magnitude numbers for 0.2σ and 0.4σ are not individually given (only the 11–29% range); no absolute IID baseline referenced for the RWN-F fraction computation is shown explicitly.

Q8.answer: Within this synthetic setting and at fixed (capacity-matched) model size, per-window renormalization removes most of the level-shift-induced MAE inflation for moderate shifts (≤0.6σ) at no in-distribution cost, and roughly one third of that improvement comes from continued adaptation while two thirds comes from a single re-estimation. This is consistent with stale normalization statistics, rather than model capacity, being the main driver of level-shift error in this regime.
Q8.missing: The 'staleness dominates' interpretation is only supported because capacity was held fixed, not varied, so it establishes consistency, not that capacity is irrelevant.

Q9.answer: It does not establish: any benefit at large shifts (0.8σ), any transfer to non-synthetic/real data or to larger backbones, that capacity is genuinely unimportant (capacity was fixed, not varied), robustness to other drift types (variance or seasonality drift), or that the chosen window length is near-optimal (it was untuned).
Q9.missing: No sensitivity analysis over window length, model size, or drift type is provided to bound these gaps.

Q10.answer: The primary contribution is capacity-matched evidence that per-window renormalization (RWN) yields an 11–29% MAE reduction under moderate level shift (up to 0.6σ) at in-distribution parity, plus an ablation (RWN-F) attributing about one third of the gain to continued adaptivity and identifying a boundary at 0.8σ where the gain disappears.
Q10.missing: None major; contribution is clearly stated.

Q11.answer: Limitations: results are synthetic-only (SynthLoad), the normalization window is untuned, only level shift is studied (no variance or seasonality drift), capacity was fixed rather than varied (so the staleness-vs-capacity claim is bounded), a single small MLP backbone was used, and no gain is shown at 0.8σ.
Q11.missing: Sample-size/statistical-power considerations beyond 5 seeds are not discussed.

Q12.answer: Re-normalizing each input window with its own recent statistics removes most of the error caused by moderate post-training level shifts at no cost when there is no shift, and most of that benefit comes from re-estimating the statistics once rather than continually adapting them—but this is shown only on synthetic data and it stops helping at large (0.8σ) shifts.
Q12.missing: The one-line takeaway is buried under undefined jargon and would be hard for the stated non-specialist audience to extract.

location.quote: We ask whether RWN, i.e. per-window moment re-estimation, eliminates the LS-induced MAE inflation without IID-regime degradation.

findings.observed: The core problem is stated but only via a dense chain of acronyms (RWN, LS, MAE, IID) with 'RWN' the only one expanded inline.
findings.reader_struggle: An adjacent-domain reader must decode multiple undefined terms before grasping the question.
findings.likely_consequence: The problem is understood by specialists but obscured for the stated non-specialist audience.
findings.revision_principle: State the problem once in plain language before introducing any abbreviation.

findings.likely_consequence: The relevance of the setup to the claimed real-world problem is unclear.

location.quote: RWN removes most of it for moderate LS at IID parity, but not at 0.8σ.

The objective centers on a practical question (does per-window normalization help under level shift), but two of the motivating claims that make it a 'problem' are unsupported [CITATION NEEDED], so the 'why it matters' portion is not yet delivered to the intended audience.
